headline: Paraguay's Santiago Peña is ousted and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse
standfirst: The Senate unanimously removed Paraguay's president, who was replaced by his deputy, Pedro Alliana, as prosecutors pursue him for breach of trust and influence-peddling. In Hormuz, Iran says it shot down an American drone, and Donald Trump does not rule out resuming the war.

essentials.title: Paraguay's Santiago Peña is removed and confined to his home as Pedro Alliana takes over
essentials.standfirst: The Senate on Friday removed the head of state, brought down by the collapse of Ueno bank, and his vice-president was sworn in at once. Prosecutors have ordered the former president to stay at home in an inquiry into suspected breach of trust and influence-peddling.
body: On Friday 6 November Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office, by the unanimous vote of the 44 senators present according to the Associated Press, a day after the lower house impeached him, and Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in in Asunción to serve out a term that runs until August 2028.

Prosecutors promptly ordered the former head of state to remain at home, suspecting him of breach of trust, attempted fraud and influence-peddling in the affair of Ueno bank, seized on 3 November, where the public pension fund had placed $355m beyond legal limits.

Mr Peña, whose resignation Congress refused and who thereby forfeits the life seat in the Senate promised to former presidents, was due to be questioned by prosecutors on Saturday; they have also issued an arrest warrant for the former central-bank governor, Carlos Carvallo.

analysis.title: A bank for two-thirds of adults
analysis.text: The scale of the crisis reflects Ueno's place in Paraguayans' lives. According to the Associated Press, some 3m customers, nearly two-thirds of the country's adults, lost access to their savings and cards when it was seized, and more than 1m people had opened their first account there. The fifth-largest bank by deposits, it held more than $800m of public money. Depositors are starting to be repaid, beginning with balances below 10m guaranís, about $1,600, while the state guarantee covers up to some $37,000. Prosecutors also accuse Mr Peña, a former shareholder in the parent company, of appointing a former Ueno executive to run the central bank.

keys.title: A successor under scrutiny too
keys.text: Pedro Alliana, 52, a former governor of Ñeembucú, survived an impeachment attempt by the opposition on Thursday. According to the Associated Press, prosecutors are nonetheless investigating him as well, along with officials at the central bank and the pension fund.

keys.title: The weight of Horacio Cartes
keys.text: The former president, who leads the ruling Colorado Party, publicly backed the removal of his successor. It was his faction's support that made a near-unanimous vote in both chambers possible.

keys.title: A widening inquiry
keys.text: Twenty-seven people have been charged, including Ueno's controlling shareholder, Miguel Vázquez, and six of the bank's executives are in pre-trial detention. Luxury cars, a yacht and light aircraft have been seized.

essentials.title: Iran downs an American drone over the Strait of Hormuz as Donald Trump issues threats
essentials.standfirst: The Revolutionary Guards say they destroyed an MQ-1 drone and report two more tankers ablaze, while a sailor was killed aboard a Greek-owned ship. Donald Trump says he may be forced to destroy “the rest of Iran”.
body: On Friday 6 November Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had shot down an American MQ-1 drone over Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz and reported two tankers on fire after striking mines, while the Greek owner of the Velos announced the death of a sailor hit the previous day off Qatar.

Donald Trump, who has promised to decide after the midterm elections whether to resume military operations, said he would rather not destroy the rest of Iran but might be forced to, and spoke to Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, who mediates between the two capitals.

Tehran is hardening its stance: received by Vladimir Putin on Thursday, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, repeated that the strait would stay closed until Iran's seven conditions were met, and his deputy, Ali Bagheri Kani, demands that they be implemented before any diplomacy.

impact.text: Oil prices feed through to the pump across Europe. In France, for example, diesel averaged €2.29 a litre in early November, according to AFP, despite the release of 10 million barrels from strategic stocks.

analysis.title: A selective blockade
analysis.text: The strait is not closed to everyone. According to Amir Hayat Moqaddam, a deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament's national-security committee, Indian, Chinese, Iraqi and Qatari ships pass freely, with Tehran levying transit fees on the first two, as reported by Al Jazeera. The analytics firm Kpler estimates that about 42% of Gulf crude shipped through Hormuz in October went to China and 13% to India. The arrangement spares Iran's main customers while keeping up the pressure on America's allies; Washington has imposed a naval blockade on Iran's southern ports since July. Moscow, for its part, says it is ready to support an exit from the war, and Mr Rezaei handed Vladimir Putin a letter from the Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei.

keys.title: Donald Trump's decision
keys.text: After meeting his national-security advisers, the American president said on Thursday that he would decide whether to resume strikes, according to Axios. Washington is maintaining its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

keys.title: Qatar's role
keys.text: The emirate relays messages between Washington and Tehran, including an Iranian nuclear proposal delivered on Thursday. The emir urged Donald Trump to pursue dialogue and a diplomatic solution.

keys.title: A Yemeni front
keys.text: In Yemen the Houthis, Tehran's allies, are firing missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, which since 5 October has backed an offensive by government forces. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two missiles aimed at Najran on Friday.

essentials.title: Death toll from the Komyshuvakha strike passes 50 in Ukraine ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi
essentials.standfirst: Ukraine's emergency services on Friday raised to at least 50 the death toll from the bombing of an aid centre in the Zaporizhzhia region. On the front line, Russia is barely advancing, according to the Institute for the Study of War.
body: On Friday 6 November Ukraine's State Emergency Service raised to at least 50 the death toll from the Russian strike of 2 November on an aid-distribution centre in a former school in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, where dozens of people were still missing.

Volodymyr Zelensky describes a double strike with glide bombs, which the UN human-rights monitoring mission says probably violated international law, at the end of a week in which Russia launched 2,346 drones and more than 80 missiles at Ukraine, according to Al Jazeera.

On the battlefield Russia has taken only 117 square kilometres in ten months, according to the Institute for the Study of War, while Kyiv has targeted eight Russian refineries in seven days, ahead of three-way talks scheduled for 10 and 11 November in Abu Dhabi.

analysis.title: A war of attrition that has almost stalled
analysis.text: According to the Institute for the Study of War, Russia has advanced by an average of 0.38 square kilometres a day in 2026, against 13.25 in 2025, and it even lost ground in September and October. Ukraine's general staff puts the number of Russian soldiers killed or seriously wounded between January and October at 381,300, a figure that cannot be verified. With no breakthroughs, each side is targeting the other's economy: Moscow strikes Ukraine's power grid as winter approaches, Kyiv hits Russian refineries from Yaroslavl to Ryazan. According to the Financial Times, cited by Al Jazeera, four tankers loaded with Russian diesel failed to find buyers in America despite the deal struck on 9 October between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin; the Kremlin denies this.

keys.title: The Abu Dhabi talks
keys.text: Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations are due to meet there on 10 and 11 November, at Washington's initiative. Donald Trump says a “big deal” is in the works after his contacts with the Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

keys.title: Kyiv's position
keys.text: Volodymyr Zelensky insists that no deal can be struck without Ukraine and demands lasting security guarantees. The Komyshuvakha strike came a day after the end of a local truce in Oleshky.

essentials.title: Avigdor Liberman opens the door to the ultra-Orthodox on the eve of Isaac Herzog's choice
essentials.standfirst: The leader of Yisrael Beiteinu says he is ready to govern with the ultra-Orthodox parties but rejects any government reliant on the Arab parties. Israel's president names the leader tasked with forming a government on Sunday.
body: On the eve of Sunday's nomination of the leader tasked with forming a government, Avigdor Liberman, who leads Yisrael Beiteinu, said he was open to a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties and to compromises on conscription, while vowing to vote against any government dependent on the Arab parties.

Gadi Eisenkot, recommended by 67 of the 120 members of the Knesset against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu, owes that lead to the 19 members from Ra'am and the United List, with whom three of the four parties in his bloc refuse to sit, though the bloc has only 48 seats.

The Democrats' leader, Yair Golan, speaks of “progress”, while the Likud lawmaker Miri Regev calls the rival alliance a “bloc of disaster”; the new Knesset will be sworn in on 10 November and will elect a successor to its speaker, Amir Ohana.

analysis.title: No majority without the Arab parties
analysis.text: The Knesset's arithmetic traps Gadi Eisenkot in a dilemma. Without Ra'am and the United List, his 48-member bloc falls well short of the 61 seats required; with them, he runs into the refusal of most of his allies, including Avigdor Liberman, who demands a 61-member coalition without the Arab parties and rejects any minority government supported from outside. His overture to United Torah Judaism, which recommended no one with its seven seats, does not close the gap. Mr Eisenkot also sets conditions of his own: he wants Hamas recognised as a terrorist organisation, which Ra'am's leader, Mansour Abbas, has not done, though he says he favours its disarmament. Mr Liberman, for his part, denies any rotation agreement with Mr Eisenkot.

keys.title: The timetable
keys.text: The leader named on Sunday will have 28 days, extendable by 14, to form a coalition. If that fails, a second candidate can be nominated, before a possible return to the polls.

keys.title: Gaza, a truce that does not protect
keys.text: Despite the ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, at least 1,602 Palestinians have been killed since, according to Gaza's health ministry. The envoy Tony Blair met Isaac Herzog and Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday to advance Donald Trump's plan.

essentials.title: Two new vaccines tested in DR Congo against an Ebola outbreak that has killed over 5,000
essentials.standfirst: The WHO has added two vaccines designed against the Bundibugyo strain to the trial under way in Ituri. The outbreak, the worst in the country's history, has more than 10,500 confirmed cases.
body: On Wednesday 4 November the World Health Organisation announced that two vaccines designed against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, the other by Moderna, would join the clinical trial under way in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Declared in mid-May, the outbreak, the worst in the country's history, had more than 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths by 1 November, according to WHO figures cited by the UN, and no vaccine or treatment is licensed against this strain, which kills more than half of those infected.

The Tumaini trial, launched on 23 October in Bunia, capital of Ituri province, vaccinates the contacts of patients using the so-called ring method, but its results are not expected before early 2027, while the virus has already reached Uganda and Kenya.

analysis.title: A first against the Bundibugyo strain
analysis.text: This is the first time that vaccines designed specifically against the Bundibugyo virus have been tested during an outbreak, according to the WHO. Until now the trial relied on Ervebo, licensed against a different strain, Zaire. The Oxford and Moderna candidates, recommended by an independent advisory group on the strength of preclinical and early clinical data, will join four vaccination “rings” already in place around confirmed cases, led by Congo's National Institute for Biomedical Research with Médecins Sans Frontières and Africa CDC. Another trial, launched in July, is assessing treatments, including a monoclonal antibody and remdesivir. The WHO's director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, warns, however, that vaccines alone will not end the outbreak.

keys.title: An outbreak spilling over
keys.text: Uganda recorded 20 cases before being declared free of the virus in August, and Kenya registered its first cases in October, two of them fatal. An imported case has also been reported in Nigeria.

keys.title: Travel restrictions
keys.text: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called for travel restrictions on affected countries to be lifted. He argues that they penalise those countries and discourage transparent reporting of cases.
